name: Territorial Affordance and Social Prediction Gradient — How Architectural Boundaries Create Zones of Social Predictability
short_description: Architecture creates territorial gradient from private to public; each zone has distinct social prediction demands and behavioral norms; clear boundaries enable social brain calibration; territorial collapse produces diffuse social PE
structural_pattern: Architecture creates a territorial hierarchy — a gradient of zones from fully private to fully public, each with distinct social prediction demands and behavioral norms (Newman, 1972; Goffman, 1959). NEWMAN'S TERRITORIAL GRADIENT: (1) PRIVATE ZONE — fully enclosed personal space, zero uninvited encounters, near-zero social processing load, Goffman's 'back stage'. (2) SEMI-PRIVATE — shared with small known group (~5, Dunbar's support clique), low social processing load. (3) SEMI-PUBLIC — shared with larger partially known group (~15-50, Dunbar's sympathy/affinity groups), moderate processing load, civil public behavior with community familiarity. (4) PUBLIC — shared with strangers (potentially >150, requires categorical rather than individual agent modeling). TERRITORIAL TRANSITIONS: Boundaries marked by doors, gates, material changes, level changes, thresholds (connecting to TP2). Each transition signals prediction regime change → enables social brain recalibration. FRONT STAGE / BACK STAGE (Goffman): Front stage = impression management required (high social PE load). Back stage = performance suspended (low social PE load). Buildings must provide both with clear transitions.
higher_order_principle: Architecture reduces social PE through territorial clarity. Clear zones with clear boundaries enable the social brain to generate accurate predictions about who will be present, what behavior is appropriate, and how much social monitoring is required. The territorial gradient is simultaneously a social prediction gradient, cognitive load gradient, and behavioral performance gradient. Good social design provides the full gradient with clear architectural markers at each transition.

private_zone.description: Fully enclosed personal space — bedroom, private office

semi_private_zone.description: Shared with small known group — shared apartment, pod office for 5-8

semi_public_zone.description: Shared with larger partially known group — lobby, courtyard, floor
semi_public_zone.social_prediction: Encounters with acquaintances and occasional strangers

public_zone.description: Shared with strangers — street, plaza, transit

dunbar_scale_mapping.5_intimate: Private office, small meeting room — intimate team interaction
dunbar_scale_mapping.15_close: Shared pod, open bay — close colleagues, visual access
dunbar_scale_mapping.50_friends: Floor or wing — periodic encounter, recognition
dunbar_scale_mapping.150_acquaintances: Building — occasional encounter in lobbies, cafeterias

dunbar_layers.description: Organization-scale, building co-location with floor tax

interaction_decay.description: Interaction frequency decays exponentially with distance; λ=8m means ~37% interaction at 8m, ~14% at 16m

floor_tax.description: Cross-floor distance counts as 8× horizontal distance for interaction prediction

pod_acoustic_targets.description: Acoustic enclosure for intimate (5-person) pods should achieve STC 35-40

zone_masking.description: Target background masking level for semi-private zones

causal_links.evidence_base: Newman (1972, ~4,000 citations) demonstrated clear territorial hierarchy reduces crime and antisocial behavior. PE interpretation is theoretical extension consistent with findings.
Social processing load increase from private to public supported by Frith's co-presence cost and Dunbar's layered social network model.
Goffman's (1959, ~80,000 citations) front/back stage framework widely accepted. Back-stage absence producing 'presentation fatigue' consistent with Evans's privacy-stress findings.
Newman (1972) documented withdrawal from commons in buildings with collapsed hierarchies. Altman & Chemers (1980) documented similar patterns cross-culturally.

scope_conditions: Applies to all buildings with multiple occupants and shared spaces
Number and character of zones varies by building type
Territorial norms are culturally specific — what constitutes 'private' vs 'semi-private' varies
Digital territory (virtual workspaces, chat channels) creates parallel structures not addressed
moderators: Building type: residential vs workplace vs institutional affects zone meaning and importance
Cultural norms: collectivist cultures may have different private/public boundary expectations
Length of tenure: long-term residents establish stronger territorial claims
Age and mobility: elderly and disabled more dependent on clear territorial cues
Power and status: higher-status occupants typically receive more private territory

interactions.nature: SC4 predicts encounter frequency. SOC3 predicts social quality based on territorial zone where encounters occur.
SOC2 describes privacy regulation mechanisms; SOC3 describes territorial structure organizing those mechanisms spatially.
Territorial transitions ARE thresholds — each boundary is both episodic boundary (TP2) and social prediction recalibration point (SOC3).
SOC1 describes interpersonal distance at person-to-person scale. SOC3 describes territorial framework determining spatial context for proxemic behavior.
